name: Transistor

claims.claim_text: The general-purpose small-signal jellybean transistors differ by region: the 2N3904 (NPN) and 2N3906 (PNP) are the standard parts in the United States, while the BC547, BC548 and 2N2222 fill the same role elsewhere, and house-branded equivalents such as the PN100 and PN200 are marketed as compatible with all of them.
claims.quote_verbatim: They're BC547, 548, 2N22222 is another one
claims.episode_title: Transistor Types and Where To Get Electronic Gear

claims.claim_text: For ordinary digital switching work only two or three NPN types need to be stocked; an internal component specification can be written as a set of tolerances a part must fall within, listing several qualifying manufacturer part numbers rather than mandating a single one.
claims.quote_verbatim: you need an NPN transistor, there's only two or three you really need to stock
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Lesnet - Bus Buccaneer Builder

claims.claim_text: Substituting a jellybean part such as the 2N3904 for a better-specified transistor trades circuit margin against supply risk, and is justified only where the specification has slack; on programmes with fixed specifications the part must meet them regardless of cost.
claims.quote_verbatim: this is the great-looking transistor, but I'm going to throw a 3904 in there because I know that if this one goes, I can get one later
claims.episode_title: Design Reviews Are Important - Habitual Hype Hebetude

claims.claim_text: An NPN with its emitter at ground and its base driven on sits at roughly 0.7 V base-emitter, and that fixed drop is used to back-calculate the surrounding node voltages rather than merely noted; ordinary diodes and LEDs are treated the same way, with Schottky diodes at about 0.2 V.
claims.quote_verbatim: if your emitter of an NPN is at ground, you know, the base, if it's on, if it has some kind of source into it, it's probably about 0.7

claims.claim_text: A 2N3904 in a simple circuit never needs more than about 10 mA of base current, because the device's current gain sets the collector current from the base current and the collector-emitter path has its own separate limit.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're never going to need more than 10 milliamps on the base

claims.claim_text: Data sheets for jellybean transistors have been progressively stripped back to absolute maximum ratings, the gain terms and the characteristic curves, so the numbers needed to bias a stage increasingly come from accumulated rules of thumb rather than from the sheet.
claims.quote_verbatim: because it's such a jellybean component, they don't put a lot of stuff in it anymore

claims.claim_text: A transistor whose beta has drifted slightly out of tolerance inside the most sensitive part of a circuit is among the hardest faults to find in equipment repair, because the device still functions and the symptom only appears at circuit level.
claims.quote_verbatim: one faulty transistor that happens to just have a slightly different beta than it should
claims.episode_title: Space Bound, Again - Xtreme Xtraplanetary Xenonosocomiophobia

claims.claim_text: Curve-tracing parts removed from a suspect board is an effective troubleshooting method; in one case it exposed a threshold voltage spread of about two volts that was within the part's published specification but outside the range the circuit had been designed around.
claims.quote_verbatim: It spread probably two volts

claims.claim_text: Transistor characteristics vary across production, and a build of 10 to 1,000 units typically draws from a single reel, so the parts behave alike and the spread stays hidden; at volume the design meets whole distributions of threshold voltage, and a design that assumed laboratory samples can stop working on a reel sitting at one extreme.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you build 100 of something, chances are all those transistors came from the same reel
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer

claims.claim_text: Second-sourcing a transistor widens the parameter spread a design must absorb, because two manufacturers' parts differ even when nominally equivalent; the defence is to build tolerance for variation into the design rather than to rely on any one supplier's typical values.
claims.quote_verbatim: You know, you could have two different transistors from two different manufacturers
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer

claims.claim_text: A curve tracer makes an unmarked transistor usable without identifying it: measuring its characteristics directly is sufficient to place a bias point and use it in an amplifier.
claims.quote_verbatim: I could use this transistor because I know what the characteristic, I don't need to know the part number

claims.claim_text: A single NPN with two resistors, a supply on the collector resistor and an independently set base voltage, is enough to explore biasing experimentally; with both supplies limited to five volts the device cannot be damaged, which removes the beginner's fear of destroying the part.
claims.quote_verbatim: I had a single NPN transistor, two resistors

claims.claim_text: A totem-pole digital output uses two transistors, one pulling high and one pulling low, so both edges are actively driven; an open-collector output such as I2C pulls down actively and relies on a pull-up resistor for the rising edge, which is why the falling edge is near-instantaneous on a scope and the rising edge visibly slower.
claims.quote_verbatim: all digital outputs are totem pole outputs. So, that means they have a driver and two output transistors

claims.claim_text: A CMOS inverter is two MOSFETs, N-channel and P-channel, with their gates tied together and their outputs tied together in a totem-pole arrangement; NMOS logic built the same function from three transistors of a single type and so did not need the two doping types CMOS requires.
claims.quote_verbatim: a CMOS inverter is simply two gates

claims.claim_text: A CMOS totem-pole clock output can degrade over a chip's life until the upper transistor no longer pulls high; because a totem-pole output carries no pull-up resistor there is nothing to hold the line, and the field fix is an external pull-up of around 100 ohms for a 25 MHz clock on a capacitive bus, drawing roughly 33 mA and producing a visibly stepped rising edge.
claims.quote_verbatim: the upper transistor might've failed. So it can't pull up

claims.claim_text: Logic inputs carry a maximum input slew-rate specification, around 500 ns for 74HC parts, and an edge slower than that voids the guaranteed behaviour: the device may enter a metastable state, and a clock input driven that slowly can oscillate metastably.
claims.quote_verbatim: for regular 7.4 HC or something, it's like 500 nanoseconds

claims.claim_text: In a complementary push-pull output stage, an NPN that turns off more slowly than the opposing PNP turns on produces shoot-through current straight between the rails; where faster devices are not available the switching frequency has to be reduced until the turn-off delay no longer matters, at the cost of bandwidth.
claims.quote_verbatim: the NPNs weren't turning off fast enough for the PNPs on the other side
claims.speaker: Dave Taylor
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dave Taylor - Multi-talented Meter Maker

claims.claim_text: A push-pull stage alternately switches an N-type device on top and a P-type on the bottom to drive a transformer or inductor, so power can be stepped up or down and rectified on the far side; dedicated controller chips exist to drive such discrete output pairs.
claims.quote_verbatim: you have two transistors, usually an N type on the top and a P type on the bottom

claims.claim_text: Power conversion trades efficiency against noise: holding transistors in their linear region to drive a sinusoid through a transformer gives a clean output at around 20 percent efficiency, while hard-switching the same devices is efficient but generates substantial harmonics.
claims.quote_verbatim: putting transistors in the linear region and actually driving a sinusoid through a transformer, you are burning tons of power
claims.episode_title: Google Glass, Lean Startup and VotC - Initializing Instructed Interviews

claims.claim_text: Early fuzz circuits produced distortion by underbiasing their transistors into non-linear operation; the sound was distinctive but the bias point moved with temperature, so behaviour was unpredictable in use. Later designs obtain distortion instead from diode clipping, amplifier overdrive, compression or parallel distortion chains.
claims.quote_verbatim: the older ones used underbiasing, like, you know, underbiasing the transistors to get them to sort of go non-linear
claims.speaker: Fran Blanche

claims.claim_text: Substituting a higher-bandwidth transistor into an existing stage is not automatically an improvement: the extra bandwidth amplifies noise that the slower device had attenuated, in one case degrading a clock signal.
claims.quote_verbatim: the new transistor is a higher bandwidth than the old one, so it amplifies all this junk on our clock
claims.speaker: Mark Morin
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Mark Morin of Nufern

claims.claim_text: Bench power supplies are built from discrete op-amps and transistors because no off-the-shelf chip provides adjustable voltage and current while staying stable across all loads; parts designed for other purposes, such as class-AB amplifier drivers, are sometimes pressed into the role, but only after being breadboarded and tested.
claims.quote_verbatim: That's why power supplies are all discrete design

claims.claim_text: A single-transistor follower power supply is trivial to draw and hard to make stable across the full load range, which is where the design effort concentrates; the same topology has to be re-derived separately for bipolar and MOSFET output devices.
claims.quote_verbatim: To make it stable across all loads, there's a lot of art in that

claims.claim_text: A discrete transistor in an otherwise integrated design is usually there because that node handles more power than a logic-level or opto-isolated output could, which also makes it a disproportionately likely failure point.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're using a discrete transistor, you're usually handling a little more power
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Mark Morin of Nufern

claims.claim_text: Silicon transistors respond to light, which is why dice are packaged in opaque plastic or sealed metal cans; where light reaches a die the effect shows up as subtle intermittent misbehaviour, single bits changing rather than outright failure.
claims.quote_verbatim: silicon transistors are susceptible to light
claims.episode_title: 555 Contest, Computer Museum, Octopart - The Green Pen Hornswoggle

claims.claim_text: Carriers that fail to complete the transit between source and drain emit photons, and because silicon is transparent to infrared that emission can be imaged straight through the substrate with an infrared camera, showing which transistors on a die are switching.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can take an infrared camera and you'll see the infrared photons which get emitted by the active transistors on the chip
claims.speaker: Dmitry Nedospasov

claims.claim_text: Heat from a single overloaded transistor spreads across a die at roughly one micrometre per microsecond, a rate set by the silicon itself rather than by external heat sinking.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's like one micrometer per microsecond

claims.claim_text: Silicon carbide MOSFETs cost on the order of fifty dollars per device but withstand around 600 volts with milliohm-order on-resistance and long service life, which is what justifies them against IGBTs and trench FETs in high-efficiency power conversion.
claims.quote_verbatim: they can run it like 600 volts
claims.episode_title: Solar Factories and HVDC Lines - Pollent Power Pushing

claims.claim_text: Counterfeit power transistors predate the internet: genuine high-power TO-3 parts cost ten to twenty dollars, and fakes were identified by cutting the can open, where a visibly undersized die could be seen without a microscope.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can tell because it used a little tiny piece, ant die in there

claims.claim_text: The first transistor-based wristwatch appeared in 1960 with a germanium transistor and was rejigged in the mid-1960s to run a silicon NPN with rewound coils once germanium parts became hard to obtain; a single transistor drives two coils that excite a roughly 300 Hz tuning fork, which is why the movement hums and the second hand sweeps continuously.
claims.quote_verbatim: It originally used a germanium transistor. It came out in 1960

claims.claim_text: In the discrete point-to-point era circuit simplicity was imposed by physical space rather than chosen: adding even three or four more transistors to a wristwatch-sized assembly was not feasible.
claims.quote_verbatim: even if you wanted to put like four in there, right, it starts to get space constrained real quick

claims.claim_text: In the early 1960s a single transistor cost about a week's wages, which put electronics beyond reach as a student hobby.
claims.quote_verbatim: A transistor would cost you like a week's wages
claims.speaker: Barry Marshall
claims.episode_title: Nobel Prize Winner Dr Barry Marshall

claims.claim_text: A fully characterised small-signal transistor costs about two cents, which removes device cost from most small-signal design decisions.
claims.quote_verbatim: for two cents you can buy a transistor that's fully characterized

claims.claim_text: A long-lived op-amp part number can be silently redesigned: in one case the input stage was changed from NPN to PNP front-end transistors and the 600-ohm load drive the part was known for disappeared from the data sheet, so a newly purchased part cannot be assumed to behave like the one originally designed in.
claims.quote_verbatim: The front end transistors are now PNP instead of NPN

claims.claim_text: Discrete transistors remain useful inside otherwise integrated designs for small jobs such as level shifting, and transistor-level work in the analog domain permits arrangements that cell-level design does not.
claims.quote_verbatim: I still put in individual transistors as level shifters and so forth
claims.speaker: Julia Truchsess

claims.claim_text: The guitar distortion box originated in a two-transistor circuit built to overdrive the input of a guitar amplifier, designed by a Bell Labs circuit designer and commercialised by Electro-Harmonix in the late 1960s.
claims.quote_verbatim: a two transistor circuit that would overdrive the input of a guitar amplifier
claims.speaker: Julia Truchsess

claims.claim_text: Data books once printed the internal transistor-level schematics of parts such as the 555 timer, in enough detail that the part can be rebuilt from discrete transistors and will work.
claims.quote_verbatim: you could open up a data book and they would actually show you what the internal schematic was
claims.speaker: Eric Schlaepfer
claims.episode_title: Open Circuits with Eric Schlaepfer and Windell Oskay

claims.claim_text: For a given function such as an oscillator, working down from an integrated part to an op-amp implementation and only then to discrete transistors is the more productive order to learn in, and inverts the sequence most textbooks use.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you want to do like an oscillator, you can go 555, super simple

claims.claim_text: Berkeley SPICE cannot execute the device models supplied by commercial semiconductor manufacturers: even a diode model expressed with a recombination current term will not run, and transistor models will not run at all.
claims.quote_verbatim: Berkeley Spice can't actually execute the IV curves of any commercial semiconductor
claims.speaker: Mike Engelhardt
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Mike Engelhardt - SPICE Simulator Synteresis

claims.claim_text: Because SPICE solves a non-linear system by successive linear approximation, every device model's IV curve must be continuous in both value and first derivative; every semiconductor model in Berkeley SPICE has a discontinuity somewhere, and those defects were copied into commercial simulators, including a discontinuity in PSpice's diode curve.
claims.quote_verbatim: you need to have the IV curves be continuous in value and slope
claims.speaker: Mike Engelhardt
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Mike Engelhardt - SPICE Simulator Synteresis

claims.claim_text: A typical analog switching-regulator part contains 5,000 to 8,000 transistors; simulating the first five milliseconds of its start-up transient took around 30 hours on one simulator against six hours on another, which is the difference between a result the designer can still act on and a lost day.
claims.quote_verbatim: the typical linear tech part has between 5,000 and 8,000 transistors
claims.speaker: Mike Engelhardt
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Mike Engelhardt - SPICE Simulator Synteresis

claims.claim_text: Simulation earns its place for testing a circuit concept quickly when the parts are not to hand, but a simulated design is not a validated one; low-level component behaviour is worth learning first so that simulation is not used as blind trial and error.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's quicker than breadboarding sometimes
claims.episode_title: Risky Components and Hardware Innovation - Slipshod Shack Shutdown

claims.claim_text: The 6502 contains about 3,500 transistors, and its layout was drawn by hand by one person rather than by a team.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's 3,500 transistors as a reference point
claims.episode_title: NASA, WOTW & Modular Design - The NASA Nostalgia

claims.claim_text: A NAND gate is four to six transistors, and most logic is built up from NAND gates, so gate-level design sits one abstraction above the silicon rather than at it.
claims.quote_verbatim: A NAND gate is like. Four to six transistors

claims.claim_text: Home transistor fabrication has been demonstrated with household chemicals and second-hand equipment for around a thousand dollars in materials, using a diffusion furnace; the first working device took about three years, and the natural milestones beyond a single transistor are a NAND gate and then a ring oscillator.
claims.quote_verbatim: I've been building these transistors with just household chemicals and stuff that I bought off eBay
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Carnassial Chip Chemicals

claims.claim_text: A home-fabricated transistor takes about twelve hours to produce, and a failed device costs the same twelve hours, so yield loss in a garage process is paid entirely in time rather than in materials.
claims.quote_verbatim: It takes me about, I don't know, 12 hours to make a transistor that works, and about the same amount of time to make one that doesn't work
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Carnassial Chip Chemicals

claims.claim_text: Thermal evaporation deposits interconnect metal by passing 800 to 1,000 amps through a dimpled tungsten strip holding pellets of aluminium inside a vacuum chamber; the strip reaches about 1,800 Celsius, the metal boils, and the vapour condenses on every surface in the chamber, so areas that must stay clean are masked with foil.
claims.quote_verbatim: You'll have basically a gaseous aluminum vapor cloud in the chamber that condenses and solidifies onto every surface in the chamber
claims.speaker: Sam Zeloof

claims.claim_text: Sputtering is the slower alternative to thermal evaporation: argon is flowed into the chamber and a high potential struck between a negatively biased target and the substrate, so argon ions accelerate into the target and chip off atoms that cross the low-pressure chamber and coat the substrate.
claims.quote_verbatim: the argon ions are very strongly accelerated toward the target, and they actually bombard the target and chip off little atoms
claims.speaker: Sam Zeloof

claims.claim_text: Transistor doping concentrations run in the parts-per-million to parts-per-billion range; an ion implanter sets both the depth and the number of dopant atoms precisely, whereas the diffusion available in a home setup gives far less control over either.
claims.quote_verbatim: Normally it's in the parts per million to parts per billion range
claims.speaker: Sam Zeloof

claims.claim_text: Ion implantation dopes selectively because a thick photoresist stops the beam everywhere except the opened areas; a subsequent oven step drives the implanted ions so they spread, after which the etch and resist sequence repeats for the next layer.
claims.quote_verbatim: the ions only get through where it's open
claims.episode_title: Wrong Hardware, Wrong Software - Fugacious Fan Funding

claims.claim_text: Device structure is learned faster from a labelled three-dimensional model of the silicon layers whose parts can be hidden and shown than from the top-down die photograph and cross-section drawing that textbooks supply, because the two conventional views leave the reader to reconcile them mentally.
claims.quote_verbatim: We put together Google SketchUp of the different layers in Silicon where we were able to label everything, hide everything
claims.episode_title: Wrong Hardware, Wrong Software - Fugacious Fan Funding

claims.claim_text: Layout-versus-schematic checking identifies a transistor as a gate with a diffusion on each side and requires the count in layout to equal the count in the schematic; it also enforces the fourth terminal, the body, which designers habitually tie to ground. Where separate power domains share the bulk silicon, LVS reports a soft connect through the substrate and fails the design, because that path is a latch-up risk.
claims.quote_verbatim: a transistor is defined by a gate and, you know, two, two diffusions, either side of it
claims.speaker: Anthony Wall
claims.episode_title: ADC Chip Design with Anthony Wall

claims.claim_text: A process design kit supplies a fixed set of transistor flavours, typically low, regular and high threshold voltage, which trade digital logic speed against power; the designer's remaining knobs are flavour and device size. Doping cannot be tuned as a continuous parameter, although N-wells, P-diffusions and polysilicon can be placed by hand in layout where a design needs it.
claims.quote_verbatim: you might have a low threshold voltage transistor, a regular threshold voltage transistor and a high threshold voltage transistor
claims.speaker: Anthony Wall
claims.episode_title: ADC Chip Design with Anthony Wall

claims.claim_text: A 65 nm process gives a 1.2 volt core supply, which permits only a small number of stacked gate-source voltages, and an on-chip resistor must be snaked as a long path of resistive material; together these make a transimpedance amplifier needing a large feedback resistor disproportionately expensive to integrate.
claims.quote_verbatim: that's only as so many VGSs of transistors
claims.speaker: Anthony Wall
claims.episode_title: ADC Chip Design with Anthony Wall

claims.claim_text: As processes improve, supply voltages shrink but transistor parasitic capacitances fall, which favours representing a signal in the time domain rather than the voltage domain: feeding a current into a ring oscillator yields a frequency that can be digitised directly, instead of converting the current to a voltage first.
claims.quote_verbatim: why not feed a current into a ring oscillator? And that will give you a frequency out
claims.speaker: Anthony Wall
claims.episode_title: ADC Chip Design with Anthony Wall

claims.claim_text: A switch transistor dumping charge takes roughly 70 picoseconds to do so at room temperature, and that figure moves across a minus 30 to plus 100 Celsius range, so the timing has to be characterised over temperature rather than treated as a constant.
claims.quote_verbatim: I know it will take 70 picoseconds roughly for that charge to dissipate
claims.speaker: Anthony Wall
claims.episode_title: ADC Chip Design with Anthony Wall

claims.claim_text: Integrated and board design fail in different ways: an IC designer works from about a hundred parameterised, known-good transistor types and finds it hard to commit a physical error such as a short circuit, whereas a board designer chooses among millions of parts and unverified downloaded footprints, so architectural mistakes dominate in one domain and physical ones in the other.
claims.quote_verbatim: I have maybe a hundred different types of transistor. I can change the size and the dimensions of them
claims.speaker: Anthony Wall
claims.episode_title: ADC Chip Design with Anthony Wall

claims.claim_text: Device scaling shrank intrinsic parasitic capacitances to the point where making a transistor that generates signals in the hundreds of gigahertz is routine in a state-of-the-art silicon process; at around 100 GHz the on-chip wavelength is a few hundred microns, which sets the physical dimensions of the circuitry.
claims.quote_verbatim: making a transistor that is capable of generating signals in the hundreds of gigahertz is now a trivial matter
claims.speaker: Shahriar Shahramian
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Shahriar from The Signal Path - Quisquous Quivering Quadripole

claims.claim_text: Transistor count per chip has continued to double while single-threaded performance has flattened and core count has risen, so the headline Moore's law figure no longer implies a matching gain in delivered performance.
claims.quote_verbatim: The number of transistors every year is doubling
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell
claims.episode_title: Discussing the Open Source PDK with Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: Moving to a smaller process node buys transistor density, power and speed at the cost of wafer price, manufacturing yield, leakage, radiation tolerance and possibly long-term silicon degradation, and it forces gate voltages down.
claims.quote_verbatim: you get the advantages in power consumption and speed

claims.claim_text: Bond pads shrink far more slowly than transistors, so a die on an advanced node can become pad-limited, its area set by its input-output count rather than by its circuitry.
claims.quote_verbatim: you might become pad limited because pads don't shrink nearly as fast as transistors
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Luke Beno of Analog.io

claims.claim_text: Smaller nodes impose orientation rules such as polysilicon that may run in only one direction, so IP blocks cannot be rotated; combined with the move from planar geometry to FinFET, this means an existing design cannot simply be shrunk from one node to another.
claims.quote_verbatim: your polysilicon layer, uh, has to, uh, sort of strike one way and not the other way
claims.speaker: James Adams
claims.episode_title: The RP2350 with the Raspberry Pi Team

claims.claim_text: Connecting two packaged chips on a board steps up from a 14 nm transistor through a 70 micron die pad, a package trace, a 0.5 mm pitch BGA and an 8 mil PCB trace, then back down the same ladder on the other side, roughly a millionfold expansion and contraction in feature size; eliminating those steps by placing bare die together in one package is the argument for system-in-package, at the cost of losing the ability to swap parts.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're going from a 14 nanometer transistor to a 70 micron die pad
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Craig J Bishop

claims.claim_text: Transmission electron microscope cross-sections of leading-edge transistors show features 50 to 70 atoms wide; most designs do not need that node, and analog parts such as op-amps are typically built at 250, 130 or 90 nanometres.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're literally 50 atoms wide, you know, it's nuts, 50, 70 atoms

claims.claim_text: Compact SRAM and DRAM bit cells are proprietary foundry IP, so an open process design kit forces on-chip memory to be built from ordinary transistors holding state in flip-flops, which occupies far more area; the same area cost is why adding flash or SRAM between variants of a microcontroller family is expensive.
claims.quote_verbatim: you have to use the transistors

claims.claim_text: A shared multi-project tile in the first Tiny Tapeout run measured 120 by 120 microns, enough for roughly 500 to 600 standard cells behind eight inputs and eight outputs; a schematic drawn in a browser tool is exported as a Verilog netlist and pushed automatically through the open-source flow and PDK to produce a GDS file and a report of the standard cells used.
claims.quote_verbatim: tiny tape out one, I think was 120 by 120 microns
claims.speaker: Matt Venn
claims.episode_title: Open Source Tapeout with Matthew Venn

claims.claim_text: Hand-drawn transistor-level design does not scale far: working from published papers to build a voltage reference on an open PDK, a seven-transistor circuit was already past the comfortable limit.
claims.quote_verbatim: The biggest circuit I've made so far, I think it was seven transistors. And that was too much
claims.speaker: Matt Venn

claims.claim_text: With clock speed, power and core count all saturated, additional transistors are increasingly spent on application-specific rather than general-purpose computing; that is only worthwhile where an application can bear both the up-front design cost and the ongoing maintenance.
claims.quote_verbatim: you kind of hit the top maximum speed you can hit
claims.speaker: Matt Venn

claims.claim_text: Transistors cost on the order of a nanopenny per gate, so the difference between spending twenty and twenty thousand of them is negligible and systems can be assembled at the Verilog, VHDL or IP level without regard to structural cost, until the design has to run from a battery and the cost reappears as power.
claims.quote_verbatim: transistors are on the order of a nanopinny per gate now
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Clint Cole of Digilent

claims.claim_text: Reverse-engineering a die under an optical microscope is practical up to roughly mid-1970s parts, where 50x magnification resolves the structures and the transistor count is low enough to follow; higher magnifications such as 400x introduce more problems than they solve and are needed only for far newer dies.
claims.quote_verbatim: mid-1970s is the point where I can see everything with my microscope
claims.speaker: Ken Shirriff

claims.claim_text: The working method for reading a die is to sketch on paper where the transistors are and how they are connected, then study it until the circuit resolves, simulating any sub-circuit that stays unclear in an analog simulator; the background required is period literature on the process technology of the era rather than formal training.
claims.quote_verbatim: sketching out on paper where the transistors are, how they're connected
claims.speaker: Ken Shirriff

claims.claim_text: Custom single-in-line integrated circuits of the period held dozens of transistors rather than thousands, and were decapsulated by dripping acid onto the package.
claims.quote_verbatim: single-in-line IC, you know, custom ICs, and they have, like, you know, dozens of transistors
claims.episode_title: Consolidate All The Things - Zonked Zelotic Zaitech

claims.claim_text: Failure analysis on preliminary silicon decapsulates the die and locates faulty transistors under an electron microscope; defects with a simple fix are corrected at transistor level by the test group, while faults that propagate through the system are returned to the original designers.
claims.quote_verbatim: when stuff didn't work, get a decapped and like you with the electron microscope and find like bad transistors
claims.speaker: Joe Bamberg

claims.claim_text: A scanning electron microscope images surface topography and in some cases surface composition, which makes it the standard instrument for semiconductor process diagnosis: a failed transistor taken apart and imaged will usually show what went wrong.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can take a transistor apart, put it under the microscope
claims.speaker: Adam McCombs

claims.claim_text: In printable semiconductor materials, ions mobile within the material limit switching speed and can prevent a usable on-off ratio at all, which is the main obstacle to printed transistors even where printed solar cells already work.
claims.quote_verbatim: the response time might be limited by how fast the irons can move
claims.speaker: Sam Stranks

claims.claim_text: Carbon nanotubes suspended in a liquid can be formulated as a printable ink, but printing that ink supplies only one layer of a transistor: the substrate, source, drain and gate still have to be made by other means.
claims.quote_verbatim: you do need a substrate, a source, a drain, a gate, you know, everything else still

claims.claim_text: Spin readout in a silicon quantum processor uses a modified MOSFET about 50 by 100 nanometres across, deliberately made strongly non-linear so it acts as a switch rather than a linear amplifier; displacing a single electron in its vicinity shifts its bias point by the equivalent of some tens of millivolts, which is enough to turn it from off to on.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's a small transistor that we fabricate in our clean room. It's about 50 by 100 nanometers in size
claims.speaker: Andrea Morello

claims.claim_text: When the readout transistor conducts it passes about a nanoamp, measurable in real time, so the quantum state of a single spin appears as a step in current on an oscilloscope; the spin-up state sits 1.3 kelvin, or about 120 microvolts, above the lowest energy state, which is just enough for the electron to escape the atom into the transistor's drain.
claims.quote_verbatim: it will give us about a nano-amp of current that we can measure
claims.speaker: Andrea Morello

claims.claim_text: Single dopant atoms are placed deterministically by combining an ion implanter with an atomic force microscope whose tip carries a nanometre hole and acts as a movable mask aligned to marks on the device; an on-chip detector derived from a radiation detector registers the roughly thousand electron-hole pairs created when one ion lands, and the beam is blanked immediately. It is a modification of, not a departure from, the way dopants are introduced in ordinary chips.
claims.quote_verbatim: they have an ion implanter and they've integrated that with a atomic force microscope with a tiny little nanometer hole in the tip
claims.speaker: Andrea Morello

claims.claim_text: In a classical processor information is encoded in the electrical state of a nanoscale transistor, with low and high voltage as zero and one, and logic performed by one transistor's state switching another's; a quantum computer keeps the binary logic but encodes the states in a quantum property of a suitable object, such as the spin of a dopant atom in silicon.
claims.quote_verbatim: information is encoded in the electrical state of a nanoscale transistor in silicon
claims.speaker: Andrea Morello

claims.claim_text: On-chip analog design inverts the discrete trade-off: individual integrated components are poor and their absolute spread is wide, but transistors cost nothing to add, so designs compensate for device quality by using far more devices than a discrete equivalent would.
claims.quote_verbatim: the components you have, they are totally rubbish and the spread of them are terrible
claims.speaker: Jorgen Jakobsen

claims.claim_text: Switching a transistor on and off costs a fixed quantity of charge delivered into its gate, and that gate charge is a real loss term in a switching circuit, independent of conduction loss.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's a rather large amount of, of charge that goes into that transistor

claims.claim_text: A transistor-level diagram becomes readable by recognising the standard structures inside it, such as a differential amplifier and a current source, and mapping them onto the simplified block view of the same circuit, in which the arrangement appears as an op-amp driving a transistor under feedback control.
claims.quote_verbatim: you start to see structures. You understand, right. There's like a, there's a differential amplifier in there. There's a current source

claims.claim_text: The point-contact transistor, the junction transistor and the field-effect transistor all originated at Bell Labs, which also commercialised fibre optics.
claims.quote_verbatim: the point contact transistor and the junction transistor and the field effect transistor were all, uh, Bell Labs, uh, discoveries
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer

claims.claim_text: The transistor was invented at Bell Labs' Murray Hill site in New Jersey, the organisation's research centre from the 1930s onward and still in use for research; the earlier West Street buildings in New York where the laboratories began also survive.
claims.quote_verbatim: Murray Hill is where the transistor was invented
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer

claims.claim_text: Surface states were the principal obstacle to the first point-contact transistor, and the breakthrough came when the contact tip was immersed in an electrolyte, after which amplification was observed and recorded in the laboratory notebooks. Surface states remain a limiting problem for anyone fabricating semiconductors, and point-contact devices most of all.
claims.quote_verbatim: if they immerse the tip of their contact in an electrolyte, some kind of a liquid, and I don't know what kind of liquid it was, that suddenly things started working
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer

claims.claim_text: Transistor manufacture outside AT&T was enabled by a licensing settlement obliging the company to make its technology available to other firms, which is what turned the invention into an industry rather than one company's product.
claims.quote_verbatim: basically allowed transistors to be made outside of AT&T

claims.claim_text: Successive computing device generations repeat one arc: relays reached limits of contact bounce, whole-system vibration causing bit errors elsewhere, heat and packaging; vacuum tubes then behaved almost ideally until they were pushed for speed, at which point crosstalk and propagation knowledge became essential, with the last tube machines distributing a clock from one tube to three hundred others across three buildings; transistors then shrank the packages and raised the speed, and the cycle restarted.
claims.quote_verbatim: when we invented transistors, everything shrank. The packages are smaller
claims.speaker: Howard Johnson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dr. Howard Johnson - Winsome Waveform Wizardry

claims.claim_text: Gains in serial communication speed have come primarily from the silicon rather than from connectors, cables or protocols, because smaller transistors inside the transceivers switch faster; connectors scale by simple shrinking, while cable materials set a speed-distance product through skin-effect and dielectric losses.
claims.quote_verbatim: The individual transistors inside can switch way faster than they ever could before because they're smaller
claims.speaker: Howard Johnson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dr. Howard Johnson - Winsome Waveform Wizardry

claims.claim_text: The device generally credited as the first integrated circuit, demonstrated in 1958, was two transistors on a single substrate, built by miniaturising existing transistor structures onto silicon.
claims.quote_verbatim: He had two transistors on the one substrate
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Joe Grand - Pancyclopaedic Prototyping Polymath

claims.claim_text: Bell Labs produced the first discrete transistor, while credit for the first integrated circuit is contested between Texas Instruments and Fairchild depending on how an integrated circuit is defined.
claims.quote_verbatim: They always fight over who actually did the microchip
claims.episode_title: SolidCon and Traveling Tech - Joined Junk Jocularity

claims.claim_text: A single-transistor radio built from a mail-order parts list was a standard first construction project for a hobbyist in 1957; one practitioner of that generation deliberately avoided vacuum tubes from the outset in favour of semiconductor diodes.
claims.quote_verbatim: those were the parts to build my first one transistor radio
claims.speaker: Forrest Mims
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Forrest Mims - Snell Solisequious Scientist

claims.claim_text: An AM transmitter can be built from a tank circuit and a single transistor; a second transistor is needed only where the microphone signal has to be amplified first.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can actually do it with a tank circuit and a single transistor

claims.claim_text: A super-regenerative receiver front end is a single transistor: the oscillator quenches itself at roughly half a megahertz to a megahertz, an incoming signal supplies extra energy so oscillation restarts sooner, and the resulting sawtooth is low-pass filtered, integrated and squared up through an op-amp.
claims.quote_verbatim: that active circuit, it's just – it's one transistor
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Tom LeMense - Cacaesthestic Chronometric Carriwitchet

claims.claim_text: When a board cannot be powered up, in-circuit voltage measurement is unavailable and the remaining method is to desolder components one at a time and check each in a component tester.
claims.quote_verbatim: I've already desolded one of the transistors and measured it in a transistor tester

claims.claim_text: A defect in a memory array costs one cell and can be absorbed by redundancy, whereas a defect in a processor's logic can kill the die; that asymmetry gives memory and logic different yield economics on the same process.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you lose one cell in a memory, that's not as big a deal as if you lose one transistor in a micro
claims.episode_title: Prior Art, Wafer Fabs and Guns - Whimsical Wafer Waffling

claims.claim_text: Putting flash on a die is complex and expensive to manufacture, so very high volume disposable products use mask ROM programmed during fabrication instead, alongside minimal analog such as a 4-bit ADC and a battery gauge, with the die carrying no more transistors than the function needs.
claims.quote_verbatim: That's complex and expensive to make a die with flash ROM

claims.claim_text: Every driven transistor brings a resistor with it, whether a base resistor or a pull-up for an open-collector output, which is why passive count tracks transistor count in discrete designs.
claims.quote_verbatim: every time you drive a transistor, you need a resistor
claims.episode_title: Layout, CAD & Raspberry Pi - Kedogenous Kinetic Knowledge

claims.claim_text: Recreating vintage synthesiser circuits requires the original low-grade transistors because the sound depends on their imperfections; scarcity of one specific part used in a well-known Moog design has driven its secondhand price to extreme levels.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's a particular transistor that's used in one of Bob Moog's famous designs. And it's become incredibly hard to find
claims.speaker: Kent Lundberg
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dr. Kent Lundberg - Luculent Linear Legacy

claims.claim_text: Jellybean transistors such as the 2N3904 are straightforward to manufacture and are second-sourced widely, which is why alternative catalogues carry large numbers of unfamiliar equivalents; whether the more complex parts from the same suppliers are re-engineered equivalents or direct clones is generally not documented.
claims.quote_verbatim: making a 2N35904 transistor is not hard at this point

claims.claim_text: As chip prices fall, architectural innovation shifts from integrating more transistors, which only companies with fabrication access can do, toward using more chips per board, which individuals and small teams can do; a task that once took months of bring-up per additional chip becomes a viable architecture.
claims.quote_verbatim: putting more transistors in silicon is the only companies can do
claims.speaker: Bunnie Huang
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bunnie Huang - Bunnie's Bibelot Bonification

claims.claim_text: Transistor-level custom silicon became reachable through an open-source layout program for around three thousand dollars, at a far higher learning cost than a system-level ASIC flow.
claims.quote_verbatim: you really absolutely need, you know, a transistor transistor level custom silicon, then you can do it for about three grand
claims.episode_title: FPGAs, Robots & Thermocouples - Wampum's Wavering Worth

claims.claim_text: A discrete-transistor processor built as a demonstration machine used 42,300 transistors and filled a room roughly two metres tall by ten metres long.
claims.quote_verbatim: it uses 40,000 transistors, 40, 42,300 transistors

claims.claim_text: Fabs produce test wafers carrying every process element, transistors, resistors and capacitors, in a range of sizes and individually labelled, as process characterisation structures rather than as working circuits.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's got all these transistors. It's got the resistors

claims.claim_text: A vacuum-tube amplifier is tractable to a beginner because the circuit is about five components and can be reasoned through without formal training; adding transistors to such a design is what stabilises the current sources and holds the bias conditions constant.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you look at the circuit diagram, it literally is five components
claims.speaker: Remco Stoutjesdijk
claims.episode_title: High End Audio with Remco Stoutjesdijk

claims.claim_text: The Saturn launch vehicle digital computer used hybrid modules containing only a couple of transistors each, deliberately built from established radiation-hardened technology rather than the newer integrated circuits used in the Apollo guidance computer, because the launch vehicle was needed before the command module and the schedule allowed no unproven process; the whole machine was immersed in circulating coolant held at constant temperature.
claims.quote_verbatim: these chips contain like a couple of transistors each
claims.speaker: Fran Blanche

claims.claim_text: One structured route through digital fundamentals starts at the semiconductor, builds transistors from it, gates from transistors, latches from gates, registers from latches and finally a CPU from those blocks, so each level answers the question the level above it leaves open.
claims.quote_verbatim: How do you build logic gates from transistors? How do you build a latch from logic gates?
claims.speaker: Ben Eater

claims.claim_text: In a home-fabricated process, cascading logic stages runs out after three or four transistors in a line, because the accumulated drop leaves too little output swing to drive the next stage.
claims.quote_verbatim: the maximum swing on the output is not enough to drive another transistor
claims.speaker: Sam Zeloof

claims.claim_text: Simulation effort scales with the cost of being wrong: a commercial shuttle run costs thousands of dollars per attempt and is therefore simulated exhaustively, whereas a garage process where a bad mask costs nothing supports iterating in silicon instead.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm down, I'm down $0
claims.speaker: Sam Zeloof

claims.claim_text: Pulling an open-collector output up to 12 volts where the device expects 5 volts drives its output transistor backwards, conducting through the base-collector junction in a mode the part was never designed for.
claims.quote_verbatim: that transistor gets flipped around backwards
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Bil Herd - Zany Z80 Zygology

claims.claim_text: A multimeter can be built from discrete transistors switching ranges and loads into a microcontroller ADC rather than a dedicated multimeter chipset, but everything the chipset provides, particularly autoranging and mode switching with their timing and gate-capacitance requirements, then has to be reproduced in software.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's a bunch of transistors on there that just switch in the various

claims.claim_text: Before computer layout, integrated circuit masks were laid out physically at very large scale: a room about thirty feet square held the masks on the floor with each transistor roughly three inches on a side, and reviewers walked across them in stocking feet.
claims.quote_verbatim: it would be about three inches by three inches each transistor
claims.speaker: Julia Truchsess

claims.claim_text: Printed electronics reached a cumulative hundred million printed devices at a complexity comparable to 7400-series logic, which is a few dozen to a few hundred transistors per part.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're about to cross 100 million transistors
claims.episode_title: We'll Believe It When We See It - Hiring Hypercatalectic Helpelp

claims.claim_text: A die photograph aligned against the corresponding PN-junction cross-section is the bridge between the abstract device model and the physical structure; the difficulty in learning semiconductors is translating between the top-down and cross-sectional views, which the two-dimensional teaching material does not do for the reader.
claims.quote_verbatim: doing that translation of like the top down view
claims.episode_title: Wrong Hardware, Wrong Software - Fugacious Fan Funding

claims.claim_text: Leading-edge gate widths below ten nanometres demand accuracies that are hard to grasp from the process description alone; a designer who wants only an op-amp does not need that node, and gains most of the practical benefit from far older processes.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's about seven nanometers of the TSMC or something

claims.claim_text: A NAND gate and a ring oscillator are the standard first structures targeted after a single working transistor, because they demonstrate that devices can be interconnected and that the process is fast enough to sustain oscillation.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm hoping by the end of the week, I'll have something, at least a NAND gate or with a little luck, a ring oscillator working
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Carnassial Chip Chemicals

attribution_notes: General: raw speaker labels in this bundle are swapped far more often than the attribution_reliable flag admits. In ep 18 the label 'Dave Jones' carries the US-centric 2N3904/2N3906 remarks while 'Chris Gammell' carries 'J-Car, the local company here' (Australia); the two are transposed. Because of that, ordinary device facts were left unattributed throughout and a speaker name was recorded only where the content itself fixes the identity.

ep 498 (Andrea Morello): flagged attribution_reliable=false, but the answering voice describes his own UNSW research, the on-chip single-electron-transistor readout and the Melbourne collaboration on ion implantation. Content-attributed to Andrea Morello with confidence.

ep 579: passages carrying the chip-design detail (65 nm 1.2 V rail, LVS and the body terminal, PDK threshold-voltage flavours, ring-oscillator current conversion, 70 ps switch timing, ~100 transistor types) are labelled 'Chris Gammell' but are plainly the guest's own PhD work at Tyndall. Content-attributed to Anthony Wall; the host's questions are what the label belongs to.

ep 390: the metallization, doping and logic-swing passages are Sam Zeloof's own garage process and are attributed to him. The passage labelled 'Sam Zeloof' that begins 'because Dave's not here, I'll actually talk about it frankly' is the host; the leading-node/TEM claim from it was left unattributed.

ep 424: the transistor-level-design passage labelled 'Chris Gammell' is duplicated by an identically worded passage labelled 'Julia Truchsess'; the content (designing with 4000-series CMOS, still placing individual transistors as level shifters, walking on masks in stocking feet) is the guest's. Attributed to Julia Truchsess.

ep 263: the Saturn launch vehicle digital computer passage is labelled 'Dave Jones' but the content is the guest's restoration work on that machine. Content-attributed to Fran Blanche, as is the fuzz-box underbiasing passage.
ep 222: flagged unreliable; the 12 V-on-a-5 V-open-collector story is the guest's, not the host's as labelled. The name was dropped and the claim stated neutrally.

ep 371 (Joe Bamberg), ep 431 (Adam McCombs), ep 560 (Remco Stoutjesdijk): all flagged unreliable, but each passage describes the guest's own job (silicon failure analysis, electron microscopy, vacuum-tube-to-silicon career). Content-attributed to the guests.
ep 616: the Tiny Tapeout flow description is labelled 'Chris Gammell' but describes the guest's own project. Attributed to Matt Venn.
ep 361: the passage about optical magnification is the host summarising ('as Ken said'), so no name was recorded; the die-reading method passage is Ken Shirriff's own and is attributed.
ep 93: flagged unreliable; the single-transistor super-regenerative front end was recorded without a name.
ep 302: the 'nanopenny per gate' passage is labelled with the guest but switches speaker mid-passage, so the name was dropped and the claim left as a general fact.
ep 673: the open-PDK SRAM passage mixes host and guest turns; no name recorded.
